paragraphs: The paper develops tree-based models for learning cancer progression from cross-sectional data. Its motivation is that progression can follow several pathways, while limited datasets make models with many parameters difficult to fit. The proposed Hidden-variable Oncogenetic Trees, or HOTs, retain a tree-based representation while allowing errors in the observations.

The authors also introduce structural expectation-maximization algorithms for individual HOTs and mixtures of HOTs. These algorithms learn model structure as part of fitting the data. Their distinctive guarantee concerns the maximization step: they find the structure that globally maximizes the expected complete-data log-likelihood, rather than merely finding a structure that improves that quantity. This is a guarantee about that step, not a claim that the entire learning procedure always reaches a globally optimal fit.

The reported findings distinguish the two model settings. Learning a single HOT performs very well with reasonably sized datasets. Learning mixtures requires substantially more data, at sizes the authors associate with future, cheaper technologies. Thus, the extra flexibility of mixtures comes with a stated practical demand for larger datasets.
neurips-2011-a-global-structural-em-algo.tldr: Hidden-variable oncogenetic trees accommodate observation errors and support structural EM updates that globally optimize each structure-selection step.

paragraphs: The paper treats chemical reaction prediction as a problem of ranking possible electron movements. Each mechanistic step connects an electron orbital source to an orbital sink. An existing rule-based expert system supplies training data containing 2,989 productive steps and 6.14 million nonproductive steps, giving the learning system examples of both useful and unsuccessful possibilities.

Prediction proceeds in two stages. Atom-level reactivity filters first remove 94.0% of nonproductive reactions with a false negative rate below 0.1%. An ensemble then ranks the remaining orbital interactions by their relative productivity within the chemical system. This division reduces the candidate set before applying the more detailed ranking models, without relying on explicit transformation patterns.

The ensemble places productive mechanisms perfectly at the top in 89.1% of cases. The reported figure reaches 99.9% when the top-ranked lists may contain up to four nonproductive reactions; these are different success criteria. The final system supports multistep prediction and produces reasonable predictions for some reactants and conditions beyond those handled by its rule-based data source.
neurips-2011-a-machine-learning-approach.tldr: A two-stage system filters and ranks orbital interactions to predict productive reaction mechanisms and support multistep chemical prediction.

paragraphs: The paper connects two approaches to learning related prediction tasks together. Alternating structure optimization learns a shared, low-dimensional predictive structure. Clustered multitask learning instead assumes that tasks belong to initially unknown groups, with similar tasks placed together. These descriptions suggest different ways for one task to benefit from information associated with others.

The authors establish an equivalence relationship between the two formulations. This gives a connection between learning shared predictive structure and discovering groups of related tasks. Because the clustered formulation is nonconvex, they also develop a convex relaxation, replacing the original optimization with a more tractable formulation. They then prove an equivalence between this relaxation and an existing convex relaxation of alternating structure optimization.

The connection has a computational payoff: the proposed convex clustered formulation is significantly more efficient, especially with high-dimensional data. The paper supplies three algorithms for solving it and reports benchmark experiments demonstrating their efficiency. Its contribution therefore combines a theoretical account of how task-sharing formulations relate with practical methods for solving the resulting optimization problems.
neurips-2011-clustered-multi-task-learni.tldr: The paper links shared-structure and clustered multitask learning, yielding an efficient convex formulation and three solution algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to assess network structure that remains after accounting for known node characteristics. In networks with binary links, latent-variable models describe connections through underlying Bernoulli probabilities. The authors construct conservative confidence sets for these probabilities as a function of a given partition of the nodes, providing a way to evaluate inferred residual structure.

The application concerns student friendship networks with race, gender, and school year as observed covariates. A logistic regression model combines those explanatory variables with a latent stochastic blockmodel component and node-specific effects. A stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm fits the model, allowing observed characteristics and additional network organization to enter the same analysis.

Maximum-likelihood estimates do not appear consistent in this setting, a qualification the paper explicitly retains. Nevertheless, confidence sets can be evaluated for different blockmodel partitions. This enables a qualitative assessment of the significance of estimated residual structure relative to a baseline that includes the covariates but no block structure. The contribution is therefore an uncertainty-based assessment of inferred network organization.
neurips-2011-confidence-sets-for-network.tldr: Conservative confidence sets help assess network structure left unexplained by observed covariates across different node partitions.

paragraphs: Matrix-valued data can contain dependencies both across rows and across columns. The paper studies Gaussian models that learn these two covariance structures while explicitly accounting for independent, identically distributed observation noise. This setting matters for predicting multiple outputs and for understanding relationships in data whose two axes both carry meaningful statistical structure.

The approach preserves computational tractability by exploiting the Kronecker product structure of the row and column covariance matrices. Within this framework, the authors generalize the Graphical Lasso to estimate a sparse inverse covariance among features while also modeling a low-rank confounding covariance among samples. This allows feature relationships and sample-level confounding to be considered within one model.

Biological applications demonstrate the framework with covariance models exceeding 100,000 dimensions. The authors report greater accuracy in recovering biological network structure and better reconstruction of the confounders. These findings support the practical value of incorporating sample dependencies alongside feature structure, while the structured covariance calculation makes the large modeled dimension computationally manageable.
neurips-2011-efficient-inference-in-matr.tldr: Structured Gaussian inference handles observation noise and sample confounding efficiently while improving biological network recovery in the reported applications.

paragraphs: The paper addresses Gaussian process regression when training inputs themselves are uncertain. Standard regression treats input locations as exact, but this model assumes they are corrupted by independent, identically distributed Gaussian noise. Accounting for that uncertainty changes how the model interprets discrepancies between its predictions and the observed outputs.

To keep computation tractable, the authors locally linearize the function around each input. This converts input uncertainty into an output-noise contribution proportional to the squared gradient of the posterior mean. The interpretation is that an input perturbation matters more where the predicted function changes rapidly. Where it changes slowly, the same input uncertainty has a smaller effect on the output.

Input-noise variances become additional hyperparameters learned by maximizing marginal likelihood. Training alternates between optimizing these parameters and recalculating the posterior gradient. The method also provides analytic predictive moments for Gaussian-distributed test inputs. Comparisons across several regression problems show improvements over the methods considered, supporting the usefulness of this local approximation for the evaluated noisy-input settings.
neurips-2011-gaussian-process-training-w.tldr: A local linear approximation lets Gaussian process regression learn input uncertainty as a gradient-dependent contribution to output noise.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common mathematical representation for shrinkage priors used in large regression problems. These priors control how strongly regression coefficients are pulled toward smaller values. Many promising constructions can be written as normal distributions whose scales are themselves random, but their different forms can obscure the relationships among them.

The authors introduce a new generalized beta distribution that generates a broad class of these normal scale mixtures. Several existing priors become special cases of the same construction. This encompassing hierarchy is intended to make it easier to compare competing priors, examine their properties, and identify connections that are less apparent when each prior is presented separately.

The hierarchy also provides a basis for a class of variational Bayes approximations. These are designed to make inference scale more efficiently to very large datasets. The paper thus connects a modeling contribution with a computational one: a shared family organizes shrinkage choices, while approximate inference methods use that organization to support large regression applications.
neurips-2011-generalized-beta-mixtures-o.tldr: A generalized beta hierarchy unifies many Gaussian scale-mixture shrinkage priors and supports scalable variational Bayesian inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine candidate models for least-squares regression so that predictions are not much worse than those of the best individual candidate. The relevant quantity is regret: the additional prediction error relative to that best model. This comparison remains useful when the candidates are misspecified, meaning none necessarily describes the data correctly.

The abstract highlights an established distinction between averaging and selecting models. Under misspecification, the worst-case regret for averaging decreases at order 1/n, whereas selecting one model has a rate of order 1/sqrt(n). Exponentially weighted model averaging is an important existing method that achieves the optimal 1/n average-regret rate, but the authors identify it as having limitations.

The proposed contribution is a new greedy averaging procedure intended to improve on exponential weighting. The authors prove strong theoretical guarantees and illustrate their results empirically. The significance is a new procedure for obtaining reliable combined predictions within a setting where averaging already has a favorable theoretical advantage over choosing a single candidate.
neurips-2011-greedy-model-averaging-0f54.tldr: A greedy model-averaging procedure offers theoretically supported improvements over exponential weighting for least-squares regression.

paragraphs: The paper combines multitask learning with structured-output prediction when task relationships form a hierarchy. Structured outputs require predicting related pieces together, as in sequence segmentation, and learning accurate models can demand substantial training data. The proposed formulation uses hierarchical regularization to let related tasks contribute information to one another.

Sharing information creates a computational challenge as well as a statistical opportunity. Combining the example sets of structured prediction tasks can make training prohibitively expensive. The authors therefore develop an efficient optimization algorithm based on bundle methods for the problems arising from their multitask formulation. The solver is an integral part of making hierarchical sharing practical at larger scales.

The evaluation uses gene-finding problems in computational biology. In these experiments, the solver converges much faster than previous methods, and hierarchical structured-output multitask learning clearly outperforms the non-multitask methods considered. These findings support both components of the approach: exploiting hierarchical task relationships can improve prediction, while the specialized solver helps manage the accompanying training cost.
neurips-2011-hierarchical-multitask-stru.tldr: Hierarchical regularization shares information across structured prediction tasks, with an efficient bundle-method solver and favorable gene-finding results.

paragraphs: The paper develops estimators for high-dimensional sparse linear regression when data are noisy, missing, or dependent. These settings depart from the familiar assumption of complete, noiseless, independently sampled observations. Addressing them often leads to nonconvex optimization, making it difficult to establish both the quality of an estimator and the behavior of a practical algorithm.

The authors analyze those statistical and computational questions together. They bound the statistical error associated with any global optimum and prove that projected gradient descent reaches a small neighborhood of the global minimizers in polynomial time. This separates the accuracy of the optimization target from the ability of an implementable procedure to approach it.

The statistical bounds hold with high probability at finite sample sizes. Under the same types of conditions required for statistical consistency, the optimization algorithm converges geometrically to a near-global minimizer. Simulations agree with the predicted scaling behavior. The resulting message is conditional but substantive: nonconvexity in these regression problems can coexist with useful accuracy guarantees and efficient convergence.
neurips-2011-high-dimensional-regression.tldr: Nonconvex estimators for sparse regression with imperfect data admit statistical guarantees and polynomial-time convergence to near-global solutions under stated conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to guide latent-feature discovery in nonparametric Bayesian models toward useful predictions. Its central choice is to regularize the desired posterior distributions directly. Priors influence the posterior through Bayesian inference, whereas posterior regularization provides another place to express preferences about the representations that learning should produce.

The authors combine this idea with large-margin learning in two models: infinite latent support vector machines for classification and a multitask version for learning related tasks. Both combine a nonparametric Bayesian model with a predictive objective for discovering latent features. The aim is to bring representation learning and the requirements of classification into the same inference framework.

The paper supplies efficient inference methods and evaluates the models on several benchmark datasets. The authors describe the results as appearing to demonstrate advantages inherited from both large-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics. That is qualified empirical support for the combination. The broader methodological contribution is showing how predictive requirements can act directly on Bayesian posterior inference, rather than entering solely through specially designed priors.
neurips-2011-infinite-latent-svm-for-cla.tldr: Infinite latent SVMs combine posterior regularization, large-margin prediction, and Bayesian nonparametric feature discovery for classification and multitask learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary with margin gamma when some training data are maliciously corrupted. It presents an algorithm that achieves accuracy 1 minus epsilon in time polynomial in the dimension, inverse margin, and inverse target error. The central improvement is how much malicious noise the algorithm can tolerate.

The tolerated noise rate scales as epsilon times gamma times sqrt(log(1/gamma)). Earlier efficient algorithms reached a rate scaling as epsilon times gamma. The new result therefore adds a square-root logarithmic factor to the tolerated corruption level while retaining polynomial running time. The guarantee concerns the margin-based learning setting described in the paper.

The algorithm achieves this without minimizing a convex loss function. The authors also prove that methods minimizing a convex proxy for misclassification error cannot tolerate malicious noise beyond the order of epsilon times gamma in this setting. This links the improved guarantee to a change in learning strategy and offers a partial explanation for the lower noise tolerance of earlier methods.
neurips-2011-learning-large-margin-halfs.tldr: A polynomial-time halfspace learner tolerates more malicious noise than convex-proxy minimization can handle in the stated margin setting.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes human actions in individual photographs by learning relationships between body parts and objects. It builds on a spatial pyramid bag-of-features representation, but replaces standard quantized local appearance features with discriminatively trained body-part and object detectors. This gives the action model cues tied more directly to people and the objects involved.

The next step represents spatial co-occurrences between individual body parts and objects. Because many such pairs are possible, the authors introduce a selection procedure using a linear support vector machine with a sparsity-inducing regularizer. This lets learning select useful interaction features from the large set of candidates and associate them with particular actions.

Learning action-specific interactions bypasses the difficult task of estimating an entire human body pose. The model can use relevant part-object relationships without first assembling a complete pose configuration. Experiments on consumer photographs show that the approach outperforms a strong bag-of-features baseline, supporting the value of explicitly representing interactions for the action-recognition setting evaluated.
neurips-2011-learning-person-object-inte.tldr: Selected spatial interactions between detected body parts and objects improve action recognition in photographs without requiring full-body pose estimation.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to recover the edges of a pairwise graphical model from high-dimensional data. Its starting point is a general analysis of a forward-backward greedy algorithm and whether that algorithm consistently identifies the correct sparsity pattern. Recovering the pattern means identifying which relationships are present, not simply producing a good numerical fit.

The authors apply this result to discrete graphical models through neighborhood estimation, learning the connections associated with individual nodes. They derive sufficient conditions involving sample size, maximum node degree, total problem size, and model parameters for recovering every edge with high probability. The stated sample requirement scales as d log(p), compared with d squared times log(p) for the existing convex-optimization approaches discussed.

The analysis uses restricted strong convexity, which the authors describe as typically milder than irrepresentability assumptions. The improvement therefore concerns both the sample scaling and the type of assumptions supporting recovery. Numerical simulations corroborate the theory. These results establish a conditional graph-selection guarantee for greedy learning, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every discrete graphical model.
neurips-2011-on-learning-discrete-graphi.tldr: A forward-backward greedy method recovers discrete graphical-model structure with favorable sample scaling under sufficient recovery conditions.

paragraphs: The paper provides a statistical framework for clustering methods that minimize pairwise dissimilarity within groups. Their empirical objectives have the form of degree-two U-statistics: they aggregate quantities calculated from pairs of observations. This pairwise structure makes U-process theory a natural tool for studying how clustering performance changes with sample size.

The analysis compares the clustering risk of a learned partition with the best risk available in the candidate class. Under suitable assumptions on the complexity of the sets defining those partitions, the excess risk is of order 1/sqrt(n). The guarantee therefore connects the amount of data and the richness of the partition class to the quality of the resulting clustering.

The authors also explain how results on the tail behavior of degenerate U-processes can yield tighter rate bounds. They consider model selection as well, including the choice of the number of clusters. The contribution is a general way to analyze pairwise clustering objectives and their statistical performance, with stronger rates available through more refined analysis.
neurips-2011-on-u-processes-and-clusteri.tldr: U-process theory yields conditional clustering-risk guarantees for pairwise objectives and supports tighter bounds and cluster-number selection analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse linear regression when measurements include both bounded noise and a sparse corruption vector whose nonzero values may be arbitrarily large. Its extended Lasso uses sparsity information about the regression coefficients and the corruptions simultaneously. The aim is to recover the underlying signal while also identifying the errors affecting individual measurements.

A first result establishes faithful recovery of both vectors through an extended restricted-eigenvalue property of the design matrix. A second analysis considers Gaussian design matrices with independent, identically distributed rows and covariance Sigma. In that setting, the authors establish recovery of the exact signed supports: which entries are nonzero and whether they are positive or negative.

The stated observation requirement is of order k log(p) log(n), even when the corrupted fraction is arbitrarily close to one under the analyzed conditions. The authors also show that the required amount of data for exact signed-support recovery is optimal. This is a particularly strong robustness result, tied to the specified design setting and recovery analysis.
neurips-2011-robust-lasso-with-missing-a.tldr: Extended Lasso jointly recovers sparse regression coefficients and large corruptions, with strong signed-support guarantees under the analyzed design conditions.

paragraphs: The paper combines two proposals for how neural populations might approximate uncertainty about the causes of sensory input. Sampling represents a posterior through draws from it, while variational approximation uses a more compact representation. The challenge is to preserve complex uncertainty without explicitly representing an intractably large posterior distribution.

The proposed method first selects a relevant region of the state space and then samples within it. Selection concentrates computation in regions containing substantial probability mass. Sampling retains the ability to represent multiple modes and arbitrary correlations. The neural interpretation pairs a feed-forward selection stage with dynamics implementing Markov chain Monte Carlo over the selected states.

Experiments use a sparse coding model with artificial data and image patches. The comparisons include exact expectation-maximization, selection alone, sampling alone, and the combined approach. The authors report effective and efficient inference and learning, including sparse coding applications exceeding a thousand observed and a thousand hidden dimensions. These demonstrations support the combined scheme as a robust, neurally plausible computational model.
neurips-2011-select-and-sample-a-model-o.tldr: Selecting high-probability states before sampling combines efficient posterior approximation with the ability to represent complex uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper introduces speedy Q-learning, a convergent variant designed to address slow convergence in standard Q-learning. Its target is the action-value function, which evaluates actions in states of a Markov decision process. The main contribution is a theoretical bound on how many steps are sufficient to obtain an approximately optimal action-value function with high probability.

For n state-action pairs and discount factor gamma, the stated bound is O(log(n)/(epsilon squared times (1 minus gamma) to the fourth power)). Here epsilon determines the desired accuracy. The expression makes explicit how the sufficient step count depends on the number of state-action pairs, the accuracy target, and the discount factor.

The authors show better dependence on inverse accuracy and inverse discount gap than the best available Q-learning result they discuss. Their bound also improves on existing results for the considered model-free and model-based batch Q-value iteration methods. The finding is a stronger convergence guarantee for this variant, with the comparison expressed through theoretical performance bounds.
neurips-2011-speedy-q-learning-8375e583b.tldr: Speedy Q-learning provides a convergent variant with a tighter high-probability step bound than the compared Q-learning and batch iteration results.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the estimation accuracy of a recently proposed convex tensor decomposition algorithm. Tensor decomposition is conventionally formulated through nonconvex optimization, which has made statistical performance difficult to analyze. Studying a convex formulation provides a route to connecting the structure of the true tensor with the error of its estimate.

The central result states that, under certain conditions, mean squared error scales linearly with a quantity the authors call normalized rank. This makes normalized rank a measure of tensor structure that enters the error guarantee directly. The result is conditional: the linear relationship is established within the setting covered by the analysis.

The theory extends the analysis of convex low-rank matrix estimation to tensors. Numerical experiments further show that the theoretical predictions can closely track the scaling behavior observed in practice. The paper therefore contributes both an interpretable relationship between tensor structure and estimation error and empirical evidence that this relationship captures the behavior of the analyzed convex method.
neurips-2011-statistical-performance-of-.tldr: Under stated conditions, convex tensor decomposition has mean squared error that scales linearly with the true tensor’s normalized rank.

paragraphs: The paper argues that optimization for learning should account for uncertainty in the data defining the loss. Because observations are generated stochastically, there is an intrinsic statistical scale of precision. The authors use the statistical properties of update quantities, such as gradients, to assess whether proposed optimization steps are reliable.

Their algorithms compute updates using subsets of the data and apply frequentist hypothesis tests to decide when those subsets should grow. This connects computational effort to the evidence available for an update direction. The procedure stops when the batch size reaches the full dataset, which the authors describe as providing computational benefits and avoiding overfitting.

A single interpretable parameter controls the probability of an update pointing in the wrong direction, and the same value is used across algorithms and datasets. The paper illustrates the idea with L1-regularized coordinate algorithms for squared-loss support vector machines, logistic regression, and Lasso. These examples demonstrate the approach, while the authors argue that the underlying statistical testing principle has broader applicability.
neurips-2011-statistical-tests-for-optim.tldr: Hypothesis tests assess optimization-update reliability and adapt batch sizes to reduce computation while respecting statistical precision.

paragraphs: The paper addresses dependencies that remain between components extracted from real data by independent component analysis and related methods. In particular, component variances or energies can be correlated even when the components are treated as independent. The authors build a probabilistic model that explicitly represents this form of nonlinear dependence among latent signals.

The model has two stages. One linearly mixes latent signals into the observations, as in independent component analysis. The other describes energy relationships through a linear non-Gaussian structural equation model. This second stage is closely related to divisive normalization, which reduces correlations between component energies. Together, the stages represent both how signals form observations and how their energies interact.

The formulation allows the linear mixing and energy-related interactions to be estimated without approximating the likelihood function or relying on the alternative non-principled approaches discussed by the authors. Demonstrations use synthetic data, natural images, and brain signals. These applications show the model’s applicability to several data types where energy dependence is relevant to component analysis.
neurips-2011-structural-equations-and-di.tldr: A two-stage probabilistic model combines linear signal mixing with structural equations for energy dependence, linking component analysis to divisive normalization.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the statistical accuracy of multiple kernel learning with Lp-norm constraints. Its main tool is local Rademacher complexity, a way to measure the effective richness of the relevant predictors. The authors derive an upper bound that leads to a tighter excess-risk guarantee than analyses based on global complexity.

Earlier local analyses covered only p equal to one. This work extends the treatment across the full range from one to infinity, under the assumption that feature mappings associated with different kernels are uncorrelated. A matching lower-bound result establishes tightness, giving evidence that the complexity bound captures the scale of difficulty in the analyzed setting.

The resulting excess-loss rates have order n raised to minus alpha divided by one plus alpha. Alpha is the minimum eigenvalue decay rate among the individual kernels, so the guarantee connects learning speed to the slowest such decay. The contribution is both broader coverage of norm choices and a sharper account of how kernel properties influence statistical convergence.
neurips-2011-the-local-rademacher-comple.tldr: A tight local-complexity analysis yields fast excess-risk rates for Lp multiple kernel learning under uncorrelated feature mappings.

paragraphs: The paper develops generalization guarantees for multiple kernel learning across a broad class of regularizers. Its main emphasis is on dense regularization, including Lp mixed norms, motivated by observations that sparse L1 regularization does not always perform as well. The theoretical question is how regularization choices affect the rate at which prediction error improves with more data.

The authors provide a unified tool for deriving fast learning rates under arbitrary monotone norm-type regularization. Applying it to Lp multiple kernel learning yields a rate they describe as the tightest among existing bounds. They also show that their general learning rate achieves a minimax lower bound, connecting the guarantee to a fundamental worst-case benchmark.

A further result distinguishes settings where the candidate kernel spaces have different complexities. In this inhomogeneous case, dense regularization has a better learning rate than sparse L1 regularization. This supplies a theoretical reason why retaining broader kernel contributions can be beneficial when the component spaces differ in complexity, rather than treating sparsity as uniformly preferable.
neurips-2011-unifying-framework-for-fast.tldr: A unified learning-rate analysis supports dense multiple kernel regularization, including better rates than sparse regularization for kernels with differing complexities.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a common explanation for learning objectives used when maximum likelihood is computationally difficult. Many alternatives were developed from different motivations and have different mathematical forms. The authors use an information-geometric view of parametric learning to show how a broad collection of these objectives can fit within one principle.

That principle is minimum KL contraction. It considers two distributions and an operator that contracts their Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of distributional discrepancy. Learning selects parameters to minimize the contraction induced by the transformation. Different choices of contraction operator produce different objectives, making the operator the organizing element of the framework.

The authors show that this construction encompasses contrastive divergence, noise-contrastive estimation, score matching, pseudo-likelihood, partial likelihood, and several conditional, marginal, and composite-likelihood objectives. It also includes maximum mutual information and non-local contrastive objectives. The contribution is a unifying derivation of apparently separate learning methods, allowing their objectives to be understood through a shared relationship between distributions and transformations.
neurips-2011-unifying-non-maximum-likeli.tldr: Minimum KL contraction unifies many alternatives to maximum-likelihood learning through different choices of distribution-transforming operators.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic model for high-dimensional time series, where many observed quantities change together over time. Such data arise in sensor streams, gene expression, video, and motion capture. The proposed variational Gaussian process dynamical system aims to describe these observations through a lower-dimensional latent representation while learning their temporal organization.

The method builds on variational approximations for Gaussian process latent-variable models. It performs nonlinear dimensionality reduction at the same time as learning a dynamical prior in the latent space. These two components connect the compact representation of each observation with a model of how the hidden representation varies over time, rather than treating those tasks separately.

The approach also allows the appropriate latent dimensionality to be determined automatically. This makes the size of the hidden representation part of the modeling process. Demonstrations use human motion capture data and high-resolution video sequences, showing applications to two forms of complex temporal data. The contribution is a joint framework for nonlinear representation learning, latent dynamics, and dimensionality determination.
neurips-2011-variational-gaussian-proces.tldr: A variational Gaussian process dynamical system jointly learns nonlinear low-dimensional representations, latent temporal structure, and an appropriate latent dimension.
